The cursor blinks. It is a small, steady pulse at the end of a blank page, asking nothing and everything. I have one thousand words, which sounds like a generous gift until you realize a thousand words is also a cage. It is enough to begin a story, not enough to finish a life. It is enough to say I am sorry, not enough to explain why. I still sit here and think about all the words I spent today: good morning, thank you, excuse me, I don't know, maybe later. Most vanished into air. But these words might remain.

Even now, I think about language as a kind of weather. It moves through a room, changing the temperature. A sentence can warm a person or freeze them. A word can be a door or a wall. When I was a child, I believed words were solid, like stones you could carry in your pocket. I collected strange ones: archipelago, luminous, cinnamon, hullabaloo. I said them aloud just to feel their shapes. I did not know then that words can also be weapons, or bandages, or maps that lead nowhere. I only knew the simple pleasure of naming small things.

But naming is not knowing. I can say the word ocean a thousand times and still not taste salt on my lips. I can describe grief with perfect grammar and miss the way it sits in the chest like a stone. This is the trouble with words: they are always a translation. They stand in for experience, but they are not experience. Yet we have nothing else. So we always keep trying. We write letters we never send. We whisper small prayers into the deep dark. We tell stories to children so they will not be afraid of the night.

I remember a teacher who told me that writing is thinking made visible. Now I wonder if it is more like breathing made visible, or bleeding, or building a bridge while standing on it. Every sentence is a decision. Every comma is a small pause where you can change your mind. The blank page is not empty; it is full of possible lives. I could write about a lighthouse keeper. I could write about a city underwater. I could write about you. But I keep returning to the same questions: Why do we make things? Why do we leave marks?

Maybe because marks are how we say I was here. A cave painting, a carved name, a text message sent at two in the morning. We want to be witnessed. We want to matter, even to a stranger. There is loneliness in that, but also courage. To make a thing and offer it to the world is to stand in the open. Someone might laugh. Someone might shrug. Someone might say, I felt that too. That last possibility is enough. That is the gamble. That is why I am writing, word after word, trying to reach you across the distance.

The distance is not only between people. It is between who I am and who I want to be. It is between the thought and the sentence. I write to close the gap. The gap is where the work lives. If I ever felt I had arrived, I would stop. But I have not arrived. I am on a road that keeps unfolding. There are ditches and detours. There are moments of clarity, when the right word appears like a bird landing on a branch. Then it flies away. I am left with the branch and the memory of wings.

Sometimes I think about all the words I will never write. They sit in some quiet invisible warehouse, dusty and patient. The novel I did not start. The letter I was too afraid to send. The apology that arrived too late. The love poem with no address. They are not failures, exactly. They are unlived lives. I imagine them sometimes, flickering like old film. I wonder if they miss me. I wonder if they wait for a version of me who is braver, or kinder, or simply less tired. Then I remember that this moment is also a small choice.

And I choose this. I choose the blank page over the closed notebook. I choose the imperfect sentence over silence. I choose to believe that words can still do something, even now, even here. Maybe they cannot stop a war or heal a wound or bring back the dead. But they can say, I see you. They can say, you are not alone. They can say, here is a small light. I have been saved by sentences before. A line in a book. A message from a friend. A song lyric that understood me. So I keep the door open.

The door open, the window cracked, the lamp on. Outside, the night is doing whatever night does. Somewhere a train passes. Somewhere a baby cries. Somewhere someone is reading a sentence that will change their mind. I like to think of all the words moving through the world now. They are invisible, but they are real. They are making people laugh, or cry, or pause. They are connecting strangers. They are being written by people who, like me, are not sure they have anything worth saying. And still they say it. That is beautiful. That is stubborn. That is human.

So here I am, at the end of a thousand words. I have not solved anything. I have not explained the universe. I have only made a small pattern out of breath and memory. Maybe that is what writing always is: a pattern against the dark. A way of saying, I was here, and I noticed. If you have read this far, then we have shared a room. Thank you for that. Now the words run out. The cursor still blinks. The page waits for someone else. I will go on to the next thing, carrying this count with me.
